title: Caedmon's song
hook: a shy cowherd who hid when the harp came round dreams a song of creation

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hilda of Whitby, the abbess kings came to for advice. Your line was wisdom at whitby. What did she say when you asked? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

The harp is going round the table. It's a feast night, and the custom is that everyone takes a turn: the harp comes to you, you sing something, you pass it on. One man is watching it come closer, and his stomach is in knots. He can't sing. He has never been able to. So before it reaches him, he gets up, slips out the door, and walks off into the dark, the way he always does. It's his night to look after the cattle anyway. He goes to the stable, lies down near the animals, and falls asleep. Same as every feast. Except tonight, Bede says, someone is standing beside him in his sleep, calling him by name.
screen: `HE SLIPS OUT BEFORE IT REACHES HIM.`

segments.voice: His name is Caedmon, and he works for Hilda's monastery at Whitby, where we were yesterday. The voice in the dream says: Caedmon, sing me something. And he says what he always says: I can't sing. That's why I left the feast. The voice says: all the same, you will sing for me. Caedmon asks the only question left. What should I sing? Sing the beginning of created things. And he does. In the dream, Caedmon sings verses he has never heard before, praising God as the maker of heaven and earth. In the morning he still remembers them, and he can add more. He tells the man in charge of him, who takes him straight to Hilda. She calls in her learned people. They read him a passage of scripture and send him away, and the next morning he comes back with it turned into a poem. Hilda asks him to become a monk, and he spends the rest of his life turning the Bible's stories into songs in his own English. Bede tells us one more thing. He writes his history in Latin, so he gives Caedmon's song in Latin too. But he stops to say this is only the sense of it, not the words. A poem, Bede says, can't be carried from one language into another word for word without losing its beauty. So the shy man's song has to be heard in his own tongue. Bede adds that Caedmon learned the art of singing not from people but from God.

Here's the practice: sing something small. Nobody's listening, and nobody's grading. Settle, and breathe. Then let one short line of a song come out of you, as quietly as you like. A hymn you know, a lullaby, a line from the radio, or just a hum with no words. If singing feels impossible, that's exactly where Caedmon started; just hum one note and hold it. If you pray, the song can be your prayer. If you don't, let it simply be a sound you made on purpose. Then rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Caedmon's song. The cowherd who walked out when the harp came round, and sang of creation in a dream.
Your line: even the shy sing. Today, hum or sing one line somewhere you usually wouldn't: in the car, in the kitchen, under your breath on the stairs. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Christians in England remember Caedmon as a saint and as an early poet of English, and his story from Bede is often retold when churches talk about everyone having a voice in worship.

fork.setup: you're asleep in the stable. a voice says: sing me something. you've never been able to sing. what do you say?
options: I can't. that's why I left.
fork.reveal: he says both. first, I can't sing. then, when the voice insists: what should I sing? the answer: sing the beginning of created things.

original.note: Old English: the guardian of heaven's kingdom, from the opening line of Caedmon's hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a legend about a magic song.
what it means: a man too shy to sing at a feast who, in a dream, sings of creation, and spends his life turning scripture into song.
what a scholar hears: Bede giving the song in Latin, and stopping to say a poem can't be translated word for word without losing its beauty.

sources.work: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

notes: Bede 4.24: harp passed round at feasts, Caedmon leaves; his turn to keep the cattle; the dream dialogue; the reeve takes him to Hilda; learned men test him; he becomes a monk; Bede's remark on translating verse; 'not from men but from God'. All paraphrased; confirm.
'heofonrīces weard' is the West Saxon normalized form of the hymn's first line; Northumbrian copies read differently (e.g. 'hefaenricaes uard'). Confirm the form and the pronunciation guide.
'the man in charge of him' is Bede's reeve (tun-gerefa); confirm.
howItsDone: 'an early poet of English' avoids 'the first'; confirm Caedmon's commemoration in the Church of England.
Editor: cut the empty 'and it's lovely'.
